I grew up with TNG and never had much interest in the original series. It seemed backward. An artifact of a less enlightened time.

Not sure why I thought that, but I recant.

Part of what changed my view was simple redpill indoctrination. Early last year I went for a kind of woman I don't normally go for, and realized pretty quickly that there was a lot I needed to learn. So learn I did, and along the way I gained an appreciation for another "backward" character: James Bond. I read some of the novels and came to appreciate that the world of the '60s was in many ways better than that of $current_year.

Kirk is a perfect example of why that is, and on that score much ink has been spilled by more knowledgeable people.

Then there are the little things. A lot of stuff was recycled at some point or another, and it's neat to see the callbacks. A certain nurse Chapel stands before Spock with that stunning vasoline-on-the-lens glow. The camera lingers, to let her sink in on you. Then you realize, that's Deanna Troi's mom! In the same episode, I think, Spock goes nuts for ~mysterious reasons~. You already know why, because the idea was recycled in Voyager.

The Voyager ep (and I'm hearkening to that Federalist link, here) certainly handled things differently. Spock ends up thinking he'd killed Kirk, and then returns to the ship to turn himself in to the space cops. We can't help smiling at this, having sussed out the trick Bones just played.

What did Tuvok do? Jerk off in the holodeck.

Also, the newer stuff is better than I thought

I was watching Return to Tomorrow, and stopped to begin this post. Kirk is in the transporter room talking to the other officers about the plot at hand when this episode's conspicuously attractive womanâ„¢ chimes in. Strings swell in sublime '60s style. The camera fixes on Kirk's reaction to this charming blindside.

She introduces herself and explains what she's doing here and... Wait just a goddamn minute. This is the same chick who would play Dr. Pulaski 20 years later!

It was after seeing this that I realized Muldaur's Pulaski is decidedly Bones-ish, which maybe militates against her being accepted by the audience. Pulaski disagrees with me less in those early episodes now only because I understand the intent: she's not just a smug cunt to Data for no reason, but was meant to be Bones to Data's Spock (i.e., a good-natured cunt.)
Just in case you didn't know, Chapel and Deanna Troi's mom were played by Majel Roddenberry, Gene Roddenberry's wife. I think she also did the computer voice on TNG. Probably some other stuff.

Captain Kirk and his unorthodox methods to solve problems earned him loyalty of Dr McCoy, his unlogical solutions that actually worked earned the friendship of Spock. His respect of his people earned devotion from Scotty. He had complete trust from Uhuru, Sulu, Chekov and even Yeoman Rand.

TNG is a throwback too given there's nearly 30 years since it premiered. To me TOS was always better Trek because TNG was too much about feelings (how very 80's) and the best TNG episodes were the ones more like TOS with less sitting around talking and more action. Some of my favourite Trek comes from TNG but when I look at the list of great episodes, season 1 and 2 of TOS had a very high hit rate whereas TNG didn't really get going until season 3 and even when it did the number of great episodes was low relative to the dross about family and feelings. The Borg were the saviours of TNG.

Alright so I'll ask the obvious question. How did you end up in the NEET position and how did you manage to maintain it for 3 years?

Also, what are you doing now?

It was basically a combination of several things. Chased my dreams too far (moved to New York City to become a writer and failed pretty badly), fell in love with a dying girl, and tried to shake it on my own in a very tough field during the middle of the economic meltdown of 2009-ish. I maintained it through lies partially based in reality: I couldn't find work because of the economic recession. That's what I told my parents, although I squandered every opportunity that came my way. I doubt that even McDonald's would have hired me based on my pathetic applications/cover letters/etc. I have no doubts that I was a terrible person for stringing my parents along like that, but I'd like to think that they forgive me for that. I hope.

I am in a PhD program and working full-time in a field that I love. I work approximately 60 hours a week but I don't mind doing it.
What is your day to day like? Do you like it?

My day to day routine is very similar to what most people do, except I cannot break it. Bad things happen when I break my routine, and I don't have that flexibility any more.

Wake up in the morning (must have 5-6 hours of sleep).

Eat breakfast and one cup of coffee (if I have more during the day, drink large glass of water to counteract it).

Go to work (or coffee shop or anywhere besides home even on weekends),

eat lunch (can never skip a meal).

After work, go to the gym (have to go at least every other day) or go hang out with friends, then go home and eat dinner before going to bed.

If I stick to my routine, I feel good, productive, normal. If I break some aspect of it, I make a mental note, deal with the oncoming anxiety that occurs, and try again the next day. Like or dislike has little to do with it: it's just what I need to do to function.
